title: The Internet Under the Ocean
subtitle: How invisible cables connect the world
author: Deep Ocean Technology

slides.kicker: 01 / The internet isn't in the cloud
slides.title:
THE INTERNET
UNDER THE OCEAN
slides.subtitle: How invisible cables connect the world
slides.notes: Open on the contradiction: we describe the internet as weightless and wireless. Then reveal that the physical machine is on the sea floor. Don't explain anything yet - just set the image.

slides.title:
Your message may cross an ocean
before it reaches the next screen.
slides.text: When you send a message, stream a video, or join a video call, enormous amounts of data travel through physical infrastructure - most of it under water.
slides.notes: The device in your hand is the endpoint, not the network. Everything after the cell tower is largely cable, and most of the long haul is subsea.

slides.title:
THE CLOUD
HAS A FLOOR.
slides.text: More than 600 active and planned cable systems carry data between continents beneath the sea.
slides.notes: This is the line the deck is built around. Pause on it. The background routes are conceptual, not a real cable map.

slides.title: LIGHT DOES THE TRAVELING.
slides.notes: Walk the chain down the left, then across the cross-section on the right. The key idea: nothing about the ocean journey is radio. It is light in glass, with an electrical layer only to power the repeaters.

slides.kicker: 03 / A cable is more than a wire
slides.title: BUILT TO SURVIVE THE OCEAN.

layers.label: OUTER PROTECTIVE JACKET
layers.note: An insulating polymer sheath, the outermost barrier

layers.label: ARMOR
layers.note: Steel wire; extra layers are added nearer the shore

layers.label: WATER BARRIER
layers.note: Keeps moisture away from the glass

layers.label: POWER CONDUCTOR
layers.note: Feeds the optical amplifiers along the route

layers.label: OPTICAL FIBERS
layers.note: The glass strands that actually carry the light

slides.note: Conceptual cross-section. Construction varies with cable design and environment - shore, sand, rock and deep ocean each demand different protection. For most of the crossing, a cable is about as thick as a garden hose, and the fibers are roughly the width of a human hair.
slides.notes: Resist the temptation to state a canonical build; the layers vary by manufacturer and by whether the section is buried near shore or laid on the abyssal floor.

slides.title: FROM SHORE TO SHORE.
slides.notes: The cable is buried under the seabed near shore and simply laid on the floor in the deep ocean. That single fact explains most of why fault causes differ by location.

slides.kicker: 05 / The scale is hard to see
slides.text: of submarine fiber-optic cable is believed to be in service worldwide as of early 2026.
slides.notes: For scale: that is roughly 37 times the circumference of the Earth. The number is TeleGeography's own estimate - attribute it rather than stating it as a census.

slides.title: A GLOBAL MESH.
slides.note: Conceptual node graph - not a survey of actual cable routes, and not a complete map of the network.
slides.notes: Say plainly that this is illustrative. Real route maps are stylised too - TeleGeography notes its own cable paths do not reflect precise geolocation.

slides.title:
COPPER MOVES SIGNALS.
FIBER MOVES LIGHT.

left.heading: Copper
bullets: Loses more signal over long distances.

slides.notes: Keep this proportionate. Copper still runs the last mile everywhere; the claim is only about long-haul ocean crossing.

slides.title: THE OCEAN FIGHTS BACK.
slides.note: Cables are engineered with different protection levels depending on location and risk. Fishing and ship anchors account for roughly two-thirds of all cable faults.
slides.source: ICPC data via TeleGeography, Submarine Cable FAQs
slides.notes: Deliberately not sensationalised. The ocean is hostile, but the damage is overwhelmingly caused by human activity, not by the environment itself.

slides.title: ONE BREAK CAN BECOME A GLOBAL PROBLEM.
slides.note: Networks are designed with redundancy, so traffic can often be rerouted while the damaged cable is restored. Roughly 200 faults are reported worldwide each year.
slides.source: ICPC data via TeleGeography, Submarine Cable FAQs
slides.notes: The point is pressure, not outage. Most users never notice a break, because capacity is spread across several cables by design.

slides.title:
WHEN THE CABLE BREAKS,
A SHIP GOES LOOKING.
slides.notes: A specialist vessel cuts and lifts one side of the damaged cable, splices in a new section, and re-lays it. The sea state, not the splice, usually sets the timeline.

slides.title: THE INTERNET IS PHYSICAL.
slides.text: Every digital experience depends on physical infrastructure somewhere.
slides.notes: Land on this quietly. The three bands are the whole argument of the deck in one slide.

slides.title:
THE CLOUD
IS NOT IN THE SKY.
slides.text: Much of the world's digital life travels through glass beneath the ocean.
